clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Wernicke Encephalopathy (Thiamine / Vitamin B1 Deficiency) in severe alcohol withdrawal risk evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Wernicke Encephalopathy (Thiamine / Vitamin B1 Deficiency) in severe alcohol withdrawal risk is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes urgent medical stabilization and parenteral thiamine, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: confusion, severe truncal ataxia, and bilateral lateral rectus palsy in a chronic heavy alcohol user (Wernicke Encephalopathy)

Key HPI features: 50M with severe alcohol use disorder brought to emergency department by neighbors who found him stumbling and confused in the hallway. Patient is unable to walk independently due to severe imbalance. Speech is slurred and disoriented to time and place. Denies recent head trauma. Has lived alone and consumed 1 liter of vodka daily with minimal food intake for the past 3 weeks.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 104, BP 110/68, Temp 36.6C. Neurological exam reveals: 1. Oculomotor: bilateral CN VI (lateral rectus) palsy with horizontal and vertical nystagmus and conjugate gaze paresis. 2. Cerebellar: severe wide-based truncal ataxia (unable to stand or walk without two-person support). 3. Encephalopathy: disoriented to date and location, lethargic, with confabulation when questioned on recent events. Fingerstick glucose 78 mg/dL. Head CT negative for intracranial hemorrhage or acute infarction.
Relevant background/PMH: Severe Alcohol Use Disorder, Alcoholic liver disease, Peripheral neuropathy
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Wernicke Encephalopathy (Thiamine / Vitamin B1 Deficiency) in severe alcohol withdrawal risk.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adjustment disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Acute suicidal or homicidal ideation.
management_principles: Urgent medical stabilization and parenteral thiamine
Give parenteral thiamine urgently under the local hospital protocol, with monitoring and correction of associated nutritional/electrolyte deficiencies
Administer thiamine promptly before or concurrently with carbohydrate when feasible; do not delay glucose for clinically significant hypoglycemia
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 50M malnourished chronic alcohol user presenting with acute onset of classic triad: encephalopathy, cerebellar ataxia, and oculomotor dysfunction.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 104, BP 110/68, Temp 36.6C. Neurological exam reveals: 1. Oculomotor: bilateral CN VI (lateral rectus) palsy with horizontal and vertical nystagmus and conjugate gaze paresis. 2. Cerebellar: severe wide-based truncal ataxia (unable to stand or walk without two-person support). 3. Encephalopathy: disoriented to date and location, lethargic, with confabulation when questioned on recent events. Fingerstick glucose 78 mg/dL. Head CT negative for intracranial hemorrhage or acute infarction.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Wernicke Encephalopathy (Thiamine / Vitamin B1 Deficiency) in severe alcohol withdrawal risk.
reference_soap.plan: Transfer for urgent medically supervised stabilization. Give parenteral thiamine under the local hospital protocol, with monitoring and correction of magnesium, folate, and other nutritional/electrolyte deficiencies. Administer thiamine before or with carbohydrate when feasible, but never delay treatment of clinically significant hypoglycemia. Monitor and treat alcohol withdrawal in a setting capable of frequent observation; use an objective or fixed-dose protocol with close monitoring when delirium makes symptom scoring unreliable. Obtain collateral history because the patient lacks capacity for a reliable independent history.

learning_objectives: Recognize the classic clinical triad of Wernicke Encephalopathy (encephalopathy/confusion, oculomotor dysfunction/CN VI palsy, and cerebellar truncal ataxia)
Administer IV thiamine promptly in malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients, while recognizing that treatment of clinically significant hypoglycemia must not be delayed
Differentiate reversible Wernicke Encephalopathy from irreversible Korsakoff Syndrome (characterized by chronic anterograde/retrograde amnesia and prominent confabulation)
Outline CIWA-Ar symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocols for managing concurrent acute alcohol withdrawal syndrome

must_ask.say: How much alcohol do you drink each day, and when was your last drink?
Have you been eating regularly, or mostly drinking without much food?
Have you had trouble walking steadily or felt off-balance recently?
Have you noticed double vision, and do you know where you are and what day it is?
Have you ever had seizures or hallucinations when you stopped drinking before?

history.answer: We found him stumbling and swaying in the apartment hallway, talking completely out of his head, so we brought him straight to the emergency room.
He lived completely independently before this and always recognized everyone, so he has never had dementia or memory problems in the past.
His stumbling and disorientation seemed to start yesterday and got noticeably worse over the last twenty-four hours.
He seems drowsy and slow to answer, cannot tell what day or month it is, but he hasn't mentioned seeing or hearing anything that isn't there.
He was stumbling into the hallway walls today, but we did not see him hit his head and he denies any recent falls or head trauma.
His speech is slurred and his balance is terrible, but his face looks symmetric and he can move both arms and legs.
He hasn't complained of any headache or stomach pain, and he hasn't thrown up.
No, he has never had any shaking spells, convulsions, tongue biting, or loss of bladder control.
No, he has had no fever, chills, cough, or changes in how often he urinates.
His neck moves freely without any stiffness, and bright room lights don't seem to bother him.
He doesn't have diabetes, doesn't take insulin or sugar pills, and hasn't complained of excessive thirst.
He has barely eaten anything solid for the past three weeks, mostly surviving entirely on vodka and tap water.
He doesn't take any sleeping pills, pain medications, or nerve pills, and we didn't find any pill bottles in his apartment.
He drinks about one liter of vodka every single day; his last drink was just an hour or two before we found him.
No, he has never had withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens when trying to stop drinking before.
He looks very thin and malnourished, his legs wobble when he tries to stand, and he seemed to have trouble focusing his eyes on us.
He lives alone in an apartment with central heating, and there was no gas leak, smoke, or toxic fumes.
A doctor told him a few years ago that his liver was damaged from heavy drinking, but his belly hasn't swelled up.
No, he has never been treated for depression, bipolar disorder, or psychosis.
When we asked him what was going on, he insisted he had just flown back from an out-of-town work trip yesterday.
We were terrified he was having a major stroke or bleeding in his brain because he couldn't walk straight.
He was diagnosed with alcohol use disorder, alcoholic liver disease, and nerve damage in his legs that makes his feet feel numb.
He had an appendectomy about twenty years ago, and he was once admitted overnight for alcohol intoxication.
He doesn't take any prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or dietary vitamins.
He has no known allergies to any medicines, foods, or environmental triggers.
He has smoked about one pack of cigarettes every day for the past thirty years.
He is currently unemployed, previously worked in construction, and lives by himself in an apartment.
Both of his parents had problems with heavy alcohol use; his father died of liver cirrhosis in his sixties.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and fingerstick glucose 78 mg/dL.
Lethargic and disoriented to time and place; confabulates when asked about recent events, claiming he just returned from a business conference.
Pupils equal and reactive to light; bilateral sixth nerve (lateral rectus) palsy present with coarse horizontal and vertical nystagmus and conjugate gaze paresis.
Bilateral lateral gaze weakness with intact facial symmetry and sensation; slurred speech noted without tongue deviation.
Severe wide-based truncal ataxia; unable to stand or walk without support from two examiners.
Normal and symmetric motor strength of 5/5 in all four extremities without focal unilateral weakness.
Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in a stocking distribution over both lower legs.
Diminished ankle jerk reflexes bilaterally with down-going plantar responses on both sides.
Mild fine postural tremor in both outstretched hands; asterixis is not present.
Supple neck with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs; no nuchal rigidity.
Mild scleral icterus present; conjunctivae are pale without petechiae or subconjunctival hemorrhage.
Dry oral mucous membranes with strong alcoholic odor on his breath; no tongue bite marks or lacerations.
No signs of scalp hematoma, facial contusions, or external trauma; dry skin with mild spider angiomas on the upper chest.
